To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we propose a novel cross-domain imitation learning approach that leverages Gromov-Wassserstein distance to learn from expert demonstrations in a different state-action space and we prove that our approach is optimal in certain settings.

the GWIL algorithm can be used to transfer policies from an expert to a different agent, even if the state spaces are completely different, and that it can be used to solve the problem of transferring policies from one state space to another, even if the expert and the learner have different state spaces.

(i) GWIL is a novel approach to cross-domain imitation learning; (ii) it can learn to imitate expert demonstrations from a source domain to a target domain, even if the two domains are arbitrarily related; (iii) it is based on the Gromov Wasserstein distance, a metric between probability distributions on metric spaces; (iv) it can be used to learn optimal imitation policies in a wide range of domains.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following problems:
    - How do we compare the performance of an expert and a learner when they operate in different environments?
how to learn to imitate from expert demonstrations when the agent has a different embodiment or state-action space than the expert.
the problem of cross-domain imitation learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GWIL algorithm is a promising approach to imitation learning that is able to handle different state spaces and action spaces.
GWIL is a very promising approach to imitation learning in the presence of domain shifts.
GWIL provides a general framework for imitation learning that is able to deal with a wide range of cross-domain settings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose GWIL, a method for imitation learning that uses optimal transport to learn a policy that mimics a given expert policy.

we propose GWIL, a method for cross domain imitation that uses the GW-distance to align and compare the state space of different agents and we prove that it preserves optimality under certain conditions.
GWIL is a simple and effective method for cross-domain Imitation Learning that works well for a variety of scenarios.
The main takeaway from our work is that
optimal transport provides a principled and general way of comparing states between agents.
the GW distance is a promising tool to compare and align trajectories in different domains.
the Gromov Wasserstein distance is a powerful and flexible tool to compare and align trajectories between different domains.
